# Session 4 · Bias & effect: can we trust it, how big is it?

## Week 4 · Saturday · online, 19:30-22:30

- Recap quiz on Session 3 (10 min)
- 4.1  Bias, confounding and causation (40 min)
- 4.2  Measuring disease and association, with a live 2x2 demo (25 min)
- Break (15 min), then two 2x2 calculations (15 min)
- 4.3  Beyond single studies: tests, meta-analysis, appraisal (30 min)
- Proposal builder 4: exposure, outcomes, biases (40 min), then wrap-up (5 min)

::: {.notes}
Start 19:30. Show three answers to the Session 3 exit question: a cohort, so 'associated'. It leads into confounding.

The only arithmetic today is division in a 2x2 table.

Clock: 19:30 recap, 19:40 4.1, 20:20 4.2 with demo, 20:45 break, 21:00 two calculations, 21:15 4.3, 21:45 proposal builder 4, 22:25 wrap-up.

Timing: 1 minute.
:::

## Recap quiz: three questions on Session 3

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 9 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Q1. Patients with sepsis who died are compared with survivors for the fluid they received on days 1-3. Design?
- Q2. Which design randomises whole intensive care units (ICUs) instead of patients?
- Q3. Restrictive vs usual fluids: mortality difference 95% CI -1 to +3 points. Margin +4 points. Result?
- Then re-read your own proposal sections 2.1 to 2.3 (design, setting, population): 3 min
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Answer each question in the poll, then have sections 2.1 to 2.3 ready to extend
:::

::: {.notes}
Three poll questions. Show the results, then the next slide. Ask one volunteer to explain why.

Timing: 9 minutes.
:::

## Recap quiz: answers

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Q1. Case-control]{.neu-card-title}

- People were chosen by outcome
- Then we look back at the fluid
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Q2. Cluster RCT]{.neu-card-title}

- Whole ICUs are randomised
- Not single patients
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Q3. Non-inferior]{.neu-card-title}

- The whole CI, -1 to +3
- stays below the +4 margin
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Chosen by outcome: case-control. Chosen by exposure: cohort.
:::

::: {.notes}
If someone says 'records, so cohort', ask: chosen by what happened to them or by what they received?

Timing: within the 9 minutes of the quiz.
:::

## Key words of the day

::: {.neu-intro}
Today's vocabulary. Each word comes with a picture or an example
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Can we trust it?]{.neu-card-title}

- Bias, confounding
- Effect modification
- Reverse causation
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[How big is it?]{.neu-card-title}

- Risk ratio (RR), odds ratio (OR)
- Risk difference (RD)
- Number needed to treat (NNT)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Tests]{.neu-card-title}

- Sensitivity, specificity
- Positive and negative predictive values
- ROC curve and the area under it
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Many studies]{.neu-card-title}

- Forest plot, heterogeneity
- Risk-of-bias tools
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Trust first, then size: an estimate can be very stable and still be off the truth.
:::

::: {.notes}
Bias = systematic error. In Vietnamese use 'sai lệch' or 'độ chệch', to tell it apart from 'sai số' (error in general).

Timing: 1 minute.
:::

## 4.1  Bias, confounding and causation

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Bias is systematic error. Size does not fix it.
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
Where bias comes from and, more importantly, how to prevent it. Selection, information, confounding, effect modification, causation. (40 minutes)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Stress this: researchers must know where bias can come from and, more importantly, how to prevent it.

Timing: 30 seconds.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A bigger sample shrinks random error but leaves bias untouched.
:::

::: {.notes}
Left: on target and tight, the goal. Middle: centred on the truth but scattered. That is random error, and a larger sample tightens it. Right: tight but off target. That is bias, and a larger sample does not move it.

A narrow CI says nothing about bias.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** If the sample differs from the target population, results may not transfer.
:::

::: {.notes}
Truth: 14 of 24 (58.3%) are severely ill. Our sample: 3 of 12 (25%) are severely ill. The filter removed the sickest patients, so the sample is systematically different: selection bias.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## Information bias: how the variables were measured

::: {.neu-intro}
Three common types
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
[Recall bias]{.neu-card-title}

- Cases remember better than controls
- e.g. families of patients who died remember the days before admission better
- **Fix: check against a more objective source, e.g. the medical record**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Observer bias]{.neu-card-title}

- An assessor who knows which treatment each group received judges differently
- e.g. 'ready for ICU discharge' in an unblinded fluid trial
- **Fix: blinded assessor, objective outcome**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Measurement bias]{.neu-card-title}

- The tool or the record is wrong in a systematic way
- e.g. urine output under-recorded on night shifts
- **Fix: standard definitions, a standardised device (ideally the gold standard), checked charts**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Measure exposure and outcome the same way in every group.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three common types. There are others, but all come from measuring the exposure or the outcome differently, or wrongly, between groups.

Recall bias: fix it by checking the information against a more objective source if possible, in this case the medical record.

Measurement bias in our question: urine output under-recorded on night shifts makes the balance look more positive than it is.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A confounder is linked to the exposure and causes the outcome.
:::

::: {.notes}
Confounding is another source of bias: a third factor mixes into the comparison. Here it is severity, so it is called confounding by indication.

Point to each arrow. Severity leads to more fluid and also to death, so fluid and death look linked even if fluid does no harm. A confounder is linked to the exposure, causes the outcome and is not on the pathway between them.

Timing: 3.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Compare like with like: within each severity level, fluid makes no difference.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hypothetical numbers. Crude RR 2.33. Within each severity level RR 1.0. 80 of 100 high-fluid patients were severe, but only 20 of 100 low-fluid.

Check aloud: 2 + 40 = 42 deaths, 8 + 10 = 18.

Ask: 'What would you measure at baseline to do this?' Expected: SOFA, lactate, vasopressor dose, age, comorbidity.

Timing: 3.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Confounding is a bias to remove. Effect modification is a finding to report.
:::

::: {.notes}
Left: within each severity stratum the RR is 1.00, but the crude RR is 2.33. Severity confounds, so adjust for it.

Right: RR 1.00 without ARDS and 0.60 with ARDS. The size of the effect differs between subgroups. That is effect modification: report each subgroup.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## How designs fight bias

::: {.neu-intro}
Most important: build the protection into the design. Repair what is left in the analysis
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Randomise and conceal allocation]{.neu-card-title}

- Chance decides the group
- Balances known and unknown confounders
- Nobody can predict the next allocation
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Blind]{.neu-card-title}

- Patients, clinicians, assessors, analysts
- Makes outcome measurement reliable
- At the very least: blind the assessor
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Restrict, match, adjust]{.neu-card-title}

- Restrict: include one level only, e.g. only septic shock
- Match: pair patients with the same confounder values
- Adjust: statistical methods in the analysis
- **[Only for confounders known and measured]{style="color:#B23B2E"}**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Only randomisation protects against confounders you never measured.
:::

::: {.notes}
Stress this: preventing bias in the design is the most important step. The analysis can only repair part of it.

Restriction: include only one level of a confounder (e.g. only septic shock), so it cannot differ between groups. Matching: pair patients with the same values of the confounders. Adjustment: statistical methods in the analysis. All three work only for confounders that are known and measured.

Weighting methods such as inverse probability weighting share the idea of matching: make the groups comparable on measured confounders. Hyun used restriction and propensity score matching.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Randomisation balances what we know and what we do not

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** By chance, both groups get a similar mix, even of factors nobody measured.
:::

::: {.notes}
The stars mark a factor nobody measured. Before allocation: 10 severe patients and 6 with the hidden factor (one of them severe). After randomisation: 5 severe and 3 starred in each group, by chance alone.

This balance holds on average. Small trials can still be unbalanced: Boulet had higher baseline creatinine in one arm.

Timing: 1.5 minutes.
:::

## Concealment before, blinding after

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Before: allocation concealment]{.neu-card-title}

- Nobody can predict the next allocation
- Paper 1 (Boulet): a central computer
- Protects who gets into each group
- Always possible, always required
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[After: blinding in Paper 1 (Boulet 2024)]{.neu-card-title}

- [Patients: blinded]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [Clinicians: knew the treatment]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [Outcome assessors: knew the treatment]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [Statisticians: blinded]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- The paper calls this 'single-blind'
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Concealment protects who gets in. Blinding protects how outcomes are measured.
:::

::: {.notes}
Boulet blinded the patients and the statisticians, not the clinicians or investigators. The authors call this 'single-blind' because the patients were blinded. Labels such as single- and double-blind are used in different ways, so CONSORT asks authors to say exactly who was blinded.

When clinicians cannot be blinded, blind the outcome assessor and use an objective outcome.

Poll: 'Is concealment possible when blinding is not?' Expected: yes, always.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Matching helps, but only for what was measured

::: {.neu-intro}
Paper 2 (Hyun 2023). SOFA: Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[1:1 matching]{.neu-card-title}

- Each positive-balance patient paired with a negative-balance patient similar on the measured factors (green box)
- 483, 373 and 392 pairs for days 1, 2 and 3
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#2E8B57"}
[Measured: balanced]{.neu-card-title}

- Age, sex, SOFA score, septic shock,
- comorbidities, infection site,
- fluid output
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Not measured: may still differ]{.neu-card-title}

- Type of fluid, nutrition,
- the clinician's bedside judgement
- **This is residual confounding**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Matching and adjustment cannot balance what nobody recorded.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hyun did not measure fluid type or nutrition. What is left is residual confounding, so a cohort still says 'associated with'.

Ask: 'One unmeasured factor that drives more fluid and predicts death?' Expected: clinical impression of shock, a failing heart, goals-of-care discussion.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Internal validity first, then external validity

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Internal validity]{.neu-card-title}

- **Is the answer right for the people studied?**
- Randomisation
- Concealment and blinding
- Complete follow-up
- Good measurement
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[External validity]{.neu-card-title}

- **Does it apply to my patients?**
- Boulet: age 18-85. My ICU: many over 85?
- Boulet: no dialysis. My ICU: patients on dialysis?
- Boulet: 3 ICUs in one country
- Boulet: only 4% of screened patients enrolled
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** First: is it right for the people studied? Then: does it apply to mine?
:::

::: {.notes}
A biased result applies nowhere. A valid trial in selected patients may not apply to your unit.

Ask: 'One patient group in your ICU who would not have entered Boulet?' Expected: over 85, chronic dialysis, more than 24 h on vasopressors.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Reverse causation: which came first?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[What we assume]{.neu-card-title}

- A positive fluid balance harms the kidneys
- Kidney injury then leads to death
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
[What may really happen]{.neu-card-title}

- Failing kidneys make less urine
- Less urine out makes the balance positive
- **The arrow runs the other way**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[How to check]{.neu-card-title}

- Which came first?
- Measure the exposure before the outcome starts
- Leave a gap in time, e.g. fluid balance on days 1 to 3, new kidney injury from day 4
- Prefer a cohort or an RCT to a cross-sectional study
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Before claiming X causes Y, make sure Y did not cause X.
:::

::: {.notes}
Failing kidneys make less urine, so the balance becomes positive. That is why Hyun matched on fluid output.

A gap in time in practice: measure the exposure in one window and count only outcomes that start after it. Then the outcome cannot have caused the exposure.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## From association to causation: Bradford Hill's causal viewpoints

| Viewpoint | What it asks | Applied to Paper 2 (Hyun 2023) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Strength | Is the effect big? | Moderate (HR about 1.6 to 2.1) |
| Consistency | Seen in other studies and places? | Yes, in other cohorts |
| Specificity | Does the exposure cause only this outcome? (the weakest clue) | Not useful here |
| Temporality | Did the cause come first? (the only must) | Balance before death, but reverse causation is possible |
| Dose-response (biological gradient) | More exposure, more effect? | Not shown |
| Plausibility | Is there a biological mechanism? | Yes: fluid overload, oedema, organ congestion |
| Coherence | Does it fit what we already know? | Mostly |
| Experiment | Does removing the exposure reduce the outcome? | Trials such as Boulet: no effect on deaths shown yet |
| Analogy | Do similar causes have similar effects? | Fluid overload harms in other settings |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
HR: hazard ratio. Causation is a judgement built from many clues. Temporality is the only must. Source: Hill AB. The environment and disease: association or causation? Proc R Soc Med. 1965;58(5):295-300.
:::

::: {.notes}
Viewpoints are clues, not a score. Stop at temporality (essential) and experiment (given by an RCT).

For Hyun: possible, not proven.

Poll: 'Which viewpoint does an RCT give that no cohort can?' Expected: experiment.

Timing: 4.5 minutes.
:::

## Quick quiz: Spot the bias

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 5 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Families of patients who died remember the days before ICU admission better than families of survivors
- In an unblinded fluid trial, the doctor who knows which treatment each group received decides when a patient is 'ready for ICU discharge'
- A fluid study includes only patients who stayed in the ICU for 3 days or more
- Patients with a higher lactate get more fluid and die more often
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Vote for one

- Selection bias
- Recall bias
- Observer bias
- Confounding
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One bias named for each scenario, and one fix said aloud
:::

::: {.notes}
Four-question poll. After each, ask one or two people for a fix. Answers and fixes on the next slide.

Timing: 5 minutes.
:::

## Answers: spot the bias

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Recall bias]{.neu-card-title}

- Bereaved families recall more
- Fix: check the medical record
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Observer bias]{.neu-card-title}

- The judge knows the group
- Fix: a blinded assessor
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Selection bias]{.neu-card-title}

- Early deaths are left out
- Fix: include all from admission
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Confounding]{.neu-card-title}

- Severity drives fluid and death
- Fix: randomise, or adjust
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Name the bias, then name the fix.
:::

::: {.notes}
Scenario 4 is confounding by indication. Without randomisation, measure severity and adjust for it. For scenario 3, also report the exclusions.

Timing: within the 5 minutes of the quiz. 4.1 ends here.
:::

## 4.2  Measuring disease and association

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
How common? How much more likely?
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
Prevalence, incidence, risk, and the 2x2 table behind RR, OR, RD and NNT. (25 minutes)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
4.2: about 17 minutes of slides, then the 8-minute demo.

Timing: 30 seconds.


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Prevalence = how many have it now. Incidence = how many new cases over time.
:::

::: {.notes}
Incidence needs a time period and only people at risk in the denominator.

Ask: 'Positive fluid balance today: prevalence or incidence? Kidney injury in the first week?' Expected: prevalence, incidence.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Risk = people with the outcome / people in the group.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hypothetical trial, not Boulet. Always ask 'out of how many?'.

Ask: 'Odds of dying with restriction?' Expected: 20 to 80, 0.25.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## The 2x2 table: one tool for every measure

| Hypothetical trial | Died | Survived | Total | Risk |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Restrictive | a = 20 | b = 80 | a + b = 100 | a / (a + b) = 20% |
| Usual care | c = 30 | d = 70 | c + d = 100 | c / (c + d) = 30% |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Always the same layout: exposure in rows, with the exposed (treated) group on top. Outcome in columns, with 'outcome yes' (died) on the left. Then a, b, c and d always mean the same thing.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep one layout: exposure in rows (exposed on top), outcome yes on the left. Most errors come from a table drawn the other way.

Ask: 'Boulet, death by day 28: a, b, c, d?' Expected: 6, 18, 6, 18.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## Four measures from one 2x2 table

::: {.neu-intro}
Worked example: restrictive 20/100 died, usual care 30/100 died
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Risk ratio (RR)]{.neu-card-title}

- \[a/(a+b)\] / \[c/(c+d)\]
- **20% / 30% = 0.67**
- Risk is one third lower
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Risk difference (RD)]{.neu-card-title}

- a/(a+b) - c/(c+d)
- **20% - 30% = -10%**
- 10 fewer deaths per 100 patients
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#2E8B57"}
[Number needed to treat (NNT)]{.neu-card-title}

- 1 / \|risk difference\|
- **1 / 0.10 = 10**
- Treat 10 to prevent 1 death
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Odds ratio (OR)]{.neu-card-title}

- Odds = died / survived: 20/80 vs 30/70
- (a/b) / (c/d)
- = (a x d) / (b x c)
- **(20/80) / (30/70) = 0.58**
- Odds of death 42% lower (odds, not risk)
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Ratios tell you how strong. Differences tell you how many patients.
:::

::: {.notes}
Go card by card, back to the table each time. 'One third lower' and '10 fewer per 100' are the same result. -10% here is a difference of 10 percentage points.

Odds first: the number with the outcome divided by the number without it, in the same group. Restrictive 20/80 = 0.25, usual care 30/70 = 0.43. The OR divides one by the other: 0.25 / 0.43 = 0.58. The short form (a x d) / (b x c) gives the same number.

Timing: 5 minutes.
:::

**KEY MESSAGE** NNT = 1 / risk difference: how many to treat for one to benefit.
:::

::: {.notes}
Of 10 patients on usual care, 3 die. Of 10 on the restrictive strategy, 2 die. The circled patient is the one who avoided death because of the treatment. The other 9 survived or died anyway.

NNT is an average, not a prediction for one patient.

Timing: 1.5 minutes.
:::

orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#B23B2E"/></marker></defs><line x1="900.0" y1="310.0" x2="955.0" y2="310.0" stroke="#B23B2E" stroke-width="5.56" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg><div style="position:absolute;left:78.455%;top:67.907%;width:21.138%;height:8.372%;box-sizing:border-box;display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;padding:calc(4.3 * 0.11292cqw);overflow:visible;text-align:left;align-items:stretch"><div style="font-size:calc(14 * 0.11292cqw);color:#1A1A1A">Odds ratio (OR)</div></div></div>

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** OR is close to RR only when the outcome is rare (under about 10%).
:::

::: {.notes}
With the RR fixed at 2, the OR moves away from 2 as the outcome becomes more common. ICU mortality is common, so here the OR exaggerates.

Ask: 'Our OR was 0.58 and RR 0.67. Why?' Expected: death is common.

The next slide answers 'when do we use the OR at all?'

Timing: 1.5 minutes.
:::

## Which measure for which design?

| Design | Measures you can report | Why |
|:---|:---|:---|
| RCT, cohort | Risk in each group, RR, RD, NNT (also OR, from logistic regression) | People are followed from exposure to outcome, so risk can be calculated |
| Case-control | OR only | We choose how many cases and controls, so risk cannot be calculated. The OR does not depend on that choice |
| Cross-sectional | Prevalence, prevalence ratio, OR | Exposure and outcome at one moment: no follow-up, so no risk over time |
| Time to event | Hazard ratio (HR) | Compares event rates over time (Session 6) |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
The OR is not wrong, but it overstates the effect when the outcome is common and is often misread as a risk ratio.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Report the RR and RD when the design allows. Use the OR for case-control studies and logistic regression.
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers the question 'Why not always the OR?' The design decides which measures exist. Only a design that follows people over time gives a risk.

Timing: 1.5 minutes.
:::

## Live demo: the 2x2 calculator

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#B5651D"}
LIVE DEMO · 8 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#B5651D"}
- The instructor shares the screen: 2x2\_calculator.xlsx, sheet Association
- Enter a, b, c, d from the worked example: 20, 80, 30, 70
- Read the risks, RR, RD, NNT and OR, and the plain-language lines
- Change the deaths to 2 and 3 of 100: watch the OR approach the RR
- Point at the red line: case-control data give an OR only
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
Watch for

- Same layout as the slide
- Relative vs absolute effect
- Rare outcome: OR close to RR
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#B5651D"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone has seen every measure computed from one table
:::

::: {.notes}
Script: s4\_demo.md. File: 2x2\_calculator.xlsx, pre-filled. Participants watch. Email the file afterwards.

Key moment: a = 2, c = 3. RR stays 0.67, OR becomes 0.66, NNT jumps to 100.

The calculator gives a 'risk' for case-control data, but only the OR is valid.

If sharing fails, do RR and NNT by hand.

Timing: 8 minutes. Then the break.
:::

## Exercise: two 2x2 calculations

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 15 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- Two 2x2 tables on our fluid question (exercise sheet, Part C)
- Calculation 1: a fluid trial. Calculation 2: a fluid case-control study
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Remember

- Risk = a / (a + b)
- RR = risk / risk
- NNT = 1 / risk difference
- OR = (a x d) / (b x c)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (7 min): draw both tables, do the calculations and write one plain sentence for each
:::

::: {.notes}
7 minutes: everyone works alone on both calculations. Then about 4 minutes per calculation: call on two or three people for each answer and type the table into the 2x2 calculator on screen. Ask one person to say each result in a plain sentence.

Calculation 1: risks 10% and 15%, RR 0.67, RD -5 points, NNT 20, OR 0.63. Same RR as before, lower baseline risk, so NNT doubles.

Calculation 2: OR = (24 x 64) / (16 x 16) = 6.0. No RR: the investigators chose the numbers of cases and controls. Ask about reverse causation (failing kidneys).

Most mistakes are layout. Key: s4\_solutions, Part C.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Sensitivity catches the sick. Specificity clears the healthy.
:::

::: {.notes}
A sensitive test rules out. A specific test rules in. PPV here is only 53%.

Poll: 'Screening must not miss sepsis: sensitivity or specificity first?' Expected: sensitivity.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## Predictive values: what a test result means for the patient

::: {.neu-intro}
Same 100 patients as the sensitivity slide: 18 true positives, 16 false positives, 64 true negatives, 2 false negatives
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Positive predictive value (PPV)]{.neu-card-title}

- Of those who test positive, how many have the disease?
- PPV = true positives / all positives
- **18 / (18 + 16) = 53%**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Negative predictive value (NPV)]{.neu-card-title}

- Of those who test negative, how many do not have it?
- NPV = true negatives / all negatives
- **64 / (64 + 2) = 97%**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Two directions]{.neu-card-title}

- Sensitivity, specificity: from the disease to the test
- PPV, NPV: from the test to the disease
- PPV and NPV change with prevalence (next slide)
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Sensitivity starts from the disease. The PPV starts from the test result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Patients and doctors ask the PPV question: 'I tested positive. Do I have it?' Work through both formulas with the numbers from the sensitivity slide.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A positive result means much less when the disease is rare.
:::

::: {.notes}
PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. Never borrow a PPV from a different setting.

Ask: 'Why do screening programmes use a second, more specific test?' Expected: to remove false positives.

Optional: show the 'PPV at another prevalence' box (s4\_demo.md, Part 2).

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Each cut-off trades sensitivity for specificity. AUC 0.80: a sick patient scores higher than a well one 80% of the time.
:::

::: {.notes}
Each dot is one cut-off of the same test, e.g. lactate 2 or 4 mmol/L. 'High' and 'low' refer to the value of the cut-off. A high cut-off calls few people positive: few false positives, so specificity is high, but more cases are missed. A low cut-off calls many people positive: few false negatives, so sensitivity is high.

The AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen patient with the disease has a higher test value than one without. 0.80 is good. The AUC does not choose the cut-off: that depends on the cost of a missed case versus a false positive.

Poll: 'Ruling out sepsis at triage: low or high lactate cut-off?' Expected: low.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Squares = studies, lines = CIs, diamond = pooled result, vertical line = no effect.
:::

::: {.notes}
Weight comes from the precision of each trial, mostly its size and number of events (inverse-variance method).

Four steps: line of no effect, squares (weight), lines (CI), diamond: RR 0.79 (0.64-0.98).

Every single trial crosses 1, but the pooled result does not. A CI crossing 1 shows uncertainty, not no effect.

No questions yet: the task at the end of 4.3 uses this plot.

Timing: 3.5 minutes.
:::


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** High I-squared means the studies disagree: find out why before trusting the diamond.
:::

::: {.notes}
With high heterogeneity ask why: patients, doses, timing, definitions or risk of bias. Random effects only widen the CI.

Ask: 'One reason fluid trials might disagree?' Expected: different populations, protocols or timing.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Which risk-of-bias tool for which design?

| If the study is a... | Appraise it with | Report it with | Course example |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Randomised trial | RoB 2 | CONSORT | Paper 1 (Boulet) |
| Non-randomised study of an intervention | ROBINS-I | TREND or STROBE |
| Cohort or case-control study of an exposure | Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (or ROBINS-E) | STROBE | Paper 2 (Hyun) |
| Diagnostic accuracy study | QUADAS-2 | STARD |
| Systematic review | AMSTAR 2 | PRISMA |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
RoB 2: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials. ROBINS-I / -E: risk of bias in non-randomised studies of interventions / exposures. QUADAS-2: for diagnostic accuracy studies. AMSTAR 2: for systematic reviews. The reporting guidelines are covered in Session 8.
:::

::: {.notes}
Reporting guidelines check what was reported. Risk-of-bias tools judge trust. Judge by domain, do not add up stars.

One-page version: Risk\_of\_Bias\_Tool\_Chooser.pdf.

Poll: 'Before-after QI study of a sepsis bundle: which tool?' Expected: ROBINS-I.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## The last question: are the conclusions supported by the data?

::: {.neu-intro}
Questions 7-9 of the 10-question appraisal checklist used in Session 8
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Words match the design]{.neu-card-title}

- 'Caused' needs randomisation
- Observational: 'associated with'
- Pilot: feasibility, not effect
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Numbers match the words]{.neu-card-title}

- Effect size with its 95% CI
- Relative and absolute effect
- No 'trend' for p = 0.42
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Honest limits, no spin]{.neu-card-title}

- Primary outcome reported first
- Main limitations stated
- Conclusion based on the primary result
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Read the conclusion last, and check it against the design and the numbers.
:::

::: {.notes}
Links to the 10-question checklist in Session 8 (Critical\_Appraisal\_Checklist.pdf).

Ask: 'Find one word in a title or abstract that overclaims.' Expected: 'impact', 'effect', 'reduces' in an observational study.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Exercise: read the forest plot, pick the tool

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 8 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- The forest plot of six fluid trials (exercise sheet, Part E)
- Read the plot, then choose a risk-of-bias tool for three studies
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Reminder

- Square = one study
- Line = 95% confidence interval
- Diamond = pooled result
- Tools: see the table two slides back
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (4 min): answer questions 1 to 3 and choose the tools for studies a to c
:::

::: {.notes}
4 minutes: everyone works alone. Then 4 minutes: show the forest-plot slide again and call on two or three people for each answer. Type the best sentence on the pooled result on screen.

Answers: Trial 4 has most weight (38%). Every trial crosses 1. The diamond does not: about 21% lower relative risk, upper limit near no effect. Tools: RoB 2 for Boulet, Newcastle-Ottawa or ROBINS-E for Hyun, AMSTAR 2 for a review.

Always say the CI with the diamond. If short of time, do the diamond sentence and the tools only.

Key: s4\_solutions, Part E.

Timing: 8 minutes. 4.3 ends here.
:::

## Outcomes: one primary, defined by what, how and when

::: {.neu-intro}
The running example (observational version)
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[What]{.neu-card-title}

- Death from any cause
- Not 'mortality improved'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[How]{.neu-card-title}

- Hospital record
- Phone call if discharged
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[When]{.neu-card-title}

- Day 28 after ICU admission
- The same day for every patient
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[2-3 secondary outcomes]{.neu-card-title}

- Acute kidney injury by day 7
- Ventilator-free days to day 28
- ICU length of stay
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Decide the primary outcome before you see the data, and report it first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Proposal builder 4 starts here (2 minutes on this slide, then 38).

Several primary outcomes invite cherry-picking.

Ask: 'Rewrite improve patient outcomes as a primary outcome.' Expected: e.g. new dialysis by day 28 after ICU admission, from the ICU chart.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Proposal builder 4: exposure, outcomes and biases

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#055F56"}
PROPOSAL BUILDER · 40 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#055F56"}
- Proposal Part 2, sections 2.4 to 2.6: exposure and comparator, outcomes, biases
- First the instructor writes them for the running example (15 min)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
Check your draft

- Comparator stated?
- Only one primary outcome?
- Outcome has a time point?
- Confounding by indication?
- A concrete fix for each bias?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#055F56"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (16 min): draft sections 2.4 to 2.6 for your own question (anything left: at home)
:::

::: {.notes}
15 minutes: fill in sections 2.4 to 2.6 for the running example on screen. 16 minutes: everyone drafts alone. 7 minutes: three volunteers read one bias and its fix.

Model: exposure positive balance at 72 h, comparator zero or negative, primary outcome death by day 28. Biases: severity (adjust or match), selection (consecutive patients), information (check 10% of charts). Full model in s4\_solutions, Part F.

Watch for: no comparator, three primary outcomes, 'we will be careful' as a mitigation.

Warn at 10 and 2 minutes before the end.
:::

## Session 4 in one slide

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[4.1 Trust]{.neu-card-title}

- Bias: size does not fix it
- Confounding: remove it
- Effect modification: report it
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[4.2 Size]{.neu-card-title}

- Relative: RR, OR
- Absolute: RD, NNT
- OR close to RR only if rare
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[4.3 Many studies]{.neu-card-title}

- PPV depends on prevalence
- Forest plot: read the diamond
- Right tool for the design
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Your proposal]{.neu-card-title}

- Part 2 complete
- Caused or associated?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Trust first, then size, and check that the words match the design.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask four volunteers to explain one card each. Each proposal now has Parts 1 and 2.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Wrap-up and homework

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#1F5C7A"}
DISCUSSION · 5 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#1F5C7A"}
- Exit question (in the chat): ICU patients who received more fluid died more often. Give one reason other than the fluid
- Homework: finish your own Proposal Part 2 (exposure, comparator, outcomes, biases)
- Optional: exercise sheet Parts B and D (effect modification, PPV in two settings)
- Next Saturday (Session 5): data, and the course dataset FLUID-ICU
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#1F5C7A"}
**OUTPUT** One exit answer per person, in the chat
:::

::: {.notes}
Exit answers: confounding by indication, or reverse causation (failing kidneys).

Open Session 5 with three anonymous answers.

Preview: Weeks 5-6 turn the design into data and introduce FLUID-ICU. In Session 6 each person chooses one of its questions (Q1-Q5) for their Results section.

Timing: 3 minutes. Finish at 22:30.
:::

## More practice (other examples): which bias?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A. Only patients who survived to hospital discharge are interviewed about their ICU care
- B. The nurse who knows which treatment each patient received scores their pain
- C. A scale that always reads 0.5 kg too high is used on one ward only
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Selection bias
- Observer bias
- Measurement bias
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One bias for each, typed in the chat
:::

::: {.notes}
Optional. One minute in the chat, then the next slide.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::

## Answers: which bias? (other examples)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[A. Selection bias]{.neu-card-title}

- Only survivors are asked
- Those who died are missing
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[B. Observer bias]{.neu-card-title}

- The nurse knows the treatment
- That can colour the score
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[C. Measurement bias]{.neu-card-title}

- The error hits one ward only
- So the comparison is distorted
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** An error on one side only distorts the comparison.
:::

::: {.notes}
C: a scale that is wrong on every ward shifts all values. On one ward only, it distorts the comparison.

Timing: within the 2 minutes, if used.
:::

## Other examples: find the confounder

::: {.neu-intro}
In each, a third factor drives both the exposure and the outcome
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Antibiotics and death]{.neu-card-title}

- More antibiotics, more deaths?
- **Confounder: severity of infection**
- Sicker patients get more drugs
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Dietitian and weight loss]{.neu-card-title}

- Seen by a dietitian, more weight loss?
- **Confounder: malnutrition at admission**
- The reason for referral
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Vasopressors and arrhythmia]{.neu-card-title}

- Vasopressors, more arrhythmia?
- **Confounder: depth of shock**
- Partly a drug effect too
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Ask: why did these patients receive the exposure? That reason may be the confounder.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask for the third factor before revealing it. Card 3 mixes a true effect and confounding.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::

## Likelihood ratios (LR) and reporting diagnostic studies

::: {.neu-intro}
Same test: sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[LR+ (positive test)]{.neu-card-title}

- sensitivity / (1 - specificity)
- **0.90 / 0.20 = 4.5**
- A positive result is 4.5 times as likely in the sick
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[LR- (negative test)]{.neu-card-title}

- (1 - sensitivity) / specificity
- **0.10 / 0.80 = 0.13**
- An LR above 10 or below 0.1 changes decisions most
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Report and appraise]{.neu-card-title}

- STARD: reporting checklist and flow diagram
- QUADAS-2: risk of bias
- Test it on the patients who will use it
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Likelihood ratios do not change with prevalence. Predictive values do.
:::

::: {.notes}
Concept only. LR+ 4.5, LR- 0.13. LRs do not depend on prevalence. Reporting: STARD. Appraisal: QUADAS-2.

Timing: 1.5 minutes if used.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Judge each domain. The overall risk is set by the worst domain.
:::

::: {.notes}
Illustrative. The worst domain drives the overall judgement. Boulet: D1 likely low, D2 some concerns, D4 low for fluid balance.

Unblinded is not automatically high risk.

Timing: 1.5 minutes if used.
:::

## Worked example: prevalence or incidence?

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Today]{.neu-step-label}

- 200 ward patients, 20 have a pressure injury
- Prevalence 10%
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[At risk]{.neu-step-label}

- 180 patients without an injury
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[One week]{.neu-step-label}

- 9 develop a new injury
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Incidence]{.neu-step-label}

- 9 / 180 = 5% per week
- Denominator: only those at risk
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Incidence always has a time period and only counts people at risk.
:::

::: {.notes}
The difference is the denominator: everyone today (200) vs those at risk (180) over a time period.

Timing: 1.5 minutes if used.
:::
